summary.text: 打 combines 扌, the side form of 手 ‘hand,’ with 丁 as a sound component. Its basic sense is ‘strike’; the same graph also writes dá ‘a dozen,’ a separate word associated with English dozen.

formation.text: 打 is phonosemantic: 手, written as 扌 in this position, contributes the hand/action category, while 丁 supplies a sound cue. The received New Attached analysis glosses the graph as ‘strike.’

components.text: 扌 is the conventional left-side form of 手 ‘hand.’ In 打 it contributes the hand/action category. The seal-script-style redraw shows it beside 丁; this positional form does not imply a chronological change from 手 to 扌.

丁 is the phonetic component in the received analysis. Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions for 丁 and 打 share an onset, rhyme, and nasal, supporting a sound relationship; the reconstructed details differ and do not directly record ancient speech.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison is reconstructed and system-dependent; it does not provide direct recordings or settle the precise historical relation.

sound.text: The reconstructions share onset, rhyme, and nasal, while differing in details.

history.text: The received Shuowen has 打 in its Song-era New Attached section rather than its main text. A curated image presents a modern redraw in Shuowen seal-script style, not a dated artifact or evidence of a sequence of graphic changes.

A consulted character database lists one small-seal form and no oracle-bone or bronze examples. A proposed connection to forms written with 木, possibly involving confusion or replacement, has not been established; no specific ancestor or corruption path is supported.

uncertainties.text: The earliest attestation remains unsettled. A Han-period poem is cited with 打 meaning ‘strike,’ and earlier dictionary citations and a gloss meaning roughly ‘to knock or strike out’ are discussed, but their transmission does not settle the dating or establish an earlier Shuowen text.
The older nasal reading and modern dǎ have a documented reading history, but proposed explanations for the later open-rime form compete; the evidence does not establish a single path.
A proposed comparison with Mizo dêng and Proto-Mon-Khmer *dah/*daʔ remains tentative; sound correspondences, chronology, cognacy, and borrowing direction are unresolved.

senses.text: A cited Han-period poem uses 打 for striking. Early dictionary citations and a gloss roughly meaning ‘to knock or strike out’ are also discussed, but transmission leaves the earliest attestation unsettled.

senses.period: Examples cited from the Liang period and later
senses.text: Later dated examples document uses for attacking and fighting. They establish these uses, but not a direct semantic path from one to the other or from a particular earlier sense.
A Song-period example records a use meaning ‘make’ or ‘manufacture’; its development from the striking sense is not established.
A Song example records ‘take/catch fish.’ The evidence does not show when or how this sense developed from other uses.
A Tang example documents a prepositional use marking place, direction, or time; its semantic development is not demonstrated by that example.

senses.gloss: a dozen; a unit of twelve
senses.text: Mandarin dá is a separate word for a dozen, associated with English dozen and the reported spelling 打臣. The graph was reused to write this word, rather than the sense developing from ‘strike.’ The first Chinese attestation and chronology of the intermediate form are unresolved.

developments.text: Attack and fighting uses are documented later than the cited Han-period striking use, but the examples do not prove a direct development from that sense.

limitations.text: Period examples document striking, attacking or fighting, making, catching fish, and a prepositional use, but do not establish their full chronology or direct semantic connections.
The dozen use is associated with English dozen, but its first Chinese attestation and a dated intermediate form are not established.

overview.text: 打 combines the hand form 扌 with 丁 as a sound component to write ‘strike.’ The same graph also writes dá ‘a dozen,’ a separate word associated with English dozen.

components.text: 扌 is the side form of 手 ‘hand’; here it signals the hand/action category.
丁 supplies a sound cue; the comparison shown is reconstructed, not a direct recording of ancient speech.

takeaway.text: For ‘a dozen,’ the whole graph was reused to write a different word associated with English dozen; this is not a meaning that grew from ‘strike.’

relationships.text: In 打, 扌 is the side form of 手 and contributes the hand/action category.
The received analysis assigns 丁 the phonetic role in 打, supported by reported Old Chinese reconstructions.
